title: Pressure-cooker mushroom risotto
subtitle: Earthy, vegetarian, and ready in under 20 minutes
excerpt: A deeply flavoured mushroom risotto cooked under pressure. Dried porcini add intensity; chestnut mushrooms give body. No standing over the hob, no constant stirring.
sourceNotes: Mushroom risotto is a staple of northern Italian home cooking, documented across multiple regional cuisines in Italy. The combination of dried porcini with fresh mushrooms follows the method in Marcella Hazan's Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: This does not keep or reheat well. Make and serve in one go.

content.text: Mushroom risotto takes 8 minutes at pressure. Add a few minutes for finishing and the whole dish is ready in under 30 minutes. Dried porcini soaked in hot water add depth that fresh mushrooms alone cannot match. The soaking liquid goes into the pot as part of the stock.

Chestnut mushrooms hold up well under pressure and have enough flavour to stand alongside the porcini. Slice them thickly so they do not disappear into the rice during cooking. The onion and garlic soften in the sauté phase before the rice and stock go in.
Stir cold butter and Parmesan through at the end, off the heat. Work quickly and vigorously. This turns the cooked rice into a creamy risotto rather than a pot of wet grains.

items.prepNote: soaked in 200 ml hot water for 10 minutes

content.text: Cover the dried porcini with 200 ml of hot water and leave to soak for 10 minutes. Drain through a fine sieve, reserving the soaking liquid. Roughly chop the porcini. Add the soaking liquid (excluding any grit at the bottom) to the hot vegetable stock.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium-high heat. Add the chestnut mushrooms and cook without stirring for 3 minutes until they colour. Add the onion and garlic; cook for 3 minutes more. Add the chopped porcini and stir through.

Add {{arborio-rice}} of arborio rice and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the combined stock and porcini soaking liquid, about 900 ml total. Season with salt and pepper. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 8 minutes, then quick-release.
Open the lid. Add the cold butter and Parmesan and stir vigorously for 1 to 2 minutes until the risotto is creamy and cohesive. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve straight away in warm bowls.

rows.cause: The chestnut mushrooms released their liquid during cooking rather than browning.
rows.fix: Next time, cook the mushrooms in a very hot pan without stirring. They need high heat and space to colour rather than steam. Don't crowd the pot.

rows.cause: Over-stirring after opening the lid can break down the starch further, making the texture too thick.
rows.fix: Stir just enough to incorporate the butter and Parmesan, then stop. If it thickens too much on standing, stir in a splash of hot stock before serving.

rows.cause: The soaking liquid was not added to the stock, or insufficient dried porcini were used.
rows.fix: The soaking liquid is the most intensely flavoured part. Always add it (strained). For a stronger porcini flavour, increase to 20 g of dried mushrooms.

rows.cause: The pressure cooker did not reach full pressure, or the rice was too cold when added.
rows.fix: Return the sealed pot to pressure for a further 2 minutes. Quick-release and finish with butter and cheese.

content.text: Mushroom risotto is autumn cooking, the kind of meal that fits a cold evening when the garden has wound down and the kitchen needs warmth. The pressure cooker version is particularly good for midweek because it removes the tedium without removing the result. Pair it with a green salad dressed with lemon and a glass of something Italian.
